displayQuote: Wisdom is the right use of knowledge. To know is not to be wise. Many men know a great deal, and are all the greater fools for it. There is no fool so great a fool as a knowing fool. But to know how to use knowledge is to have wisdom

answer.label: Spurgeon’s words, edited in circulation
answer.sourceLine: The Spurgeon Library’s text opens this thought with “Wisdom is, I suppose, the right use of knowledge.” It later says that knowledgeable people can be “all the more fools for what they know,” rather than the popular wording supplied here. The Spurgeon Library sermon ↗

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Wisdom is, I suppose, the right use of knowledge.
trail: The Spurgeon Library’s text opens this thought with “Wisdom is, I suppose, the right use of knowledge.” It later says that knowledgeable people can be “all the more fools for what they know,” rather than the popular wording supplied here. The Spurgeon Library sermon ↗

The sermon is dated 27 April 1871. The popular passage preserves Spurgeon’s distinction between knowing and wisely using knowledge, but it should be labelled an edited version rather than an exact transcription. Read the supporting source ↗

author.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
author.heading: About Charles Spurgeon
author.bio: Charles Spurgeon delivered The Fourfold Treasure as a Christian sermon. The familiar maxim about knowledge appears inside a discussion of Christ as wisdom, rather than an isolated secular definition.
